title: Experts react: Reading between the lines of the new US-Saudi nuclear agreement
gist: The Wall Street Journal reported that Trump approved a Section 123 civil nuclear agreement with Saudi Arabia that would restrict Riyadh to American nuclear suppliers and reportedly leaves open a US-operated 'black box' enrichment facility, subject to a two-year joint study. Four Atlantic Council experts split on it: a win for US industry over Russia and China, a nonproliferation mistake, a signal to Tehran after the Iran war, and a card spent for nothing because the deal has been de-linked from Saudi-Israel normalization.

insights.claim: Saudi Arabia has made clear it will build a civil nuclear program regardless, so the only real question was whether it would source technology from the US and its allies or from Russia or China — making a 123 agreement a win for both the US nuclear industry and the US-led nonproliferation regime.
insights.speaker: Jennifer T. Gordon
insights.so_what: Frames the deal as a competitive win for US nuclear vendors against Rosatom and CNNC — a demand channel for American reactor and fuel-cycle suppliers.
insights.locator: A win for the United States over Russia and China

insights.claim: The reported agreement would preclude Saudi Arabia from sourcing nuclear energy technologies from any entities except American companies, with potentially a secondary role for those companies' foreign suppliers.
insights.speaker: Jennifer T. Gordon
insights.so_what: An exclusive supplier clause would hand US nuclear firms a captive multi-decade market — the specific contract term to verify when text is released.
insights.quote: American companies with potentially a secondary role for some of those companies’ foreign suppliers
insights.locator: According to reports, this agreement would preclude

insights.claim: Close cooperation with the US nuclear industry and government would give Washington ongoing influence over the Saudi nuclear program, per the Wall Street Journal report.
insights.speaker: Jennifer T. Gordon
insights.so_what: Commercial entanglement is the enforcement mechanism substituting for legal safeguards — its durability depends on the supplier lock holding.
insights.quote: give the U.S. influence over the Saudi nuclear program

insights.claim: The reported agreement contains a provision that could allow a 'black box' uranium enrichment facility located in Saudi Arabia but run by US companies, with the need for it determined only after a two-year joint US-Saudi study.
insights.speaker: Jennifer T. Gordon
insights.so_what: The two-year study is the decision point that determines whether this becomes a proliferation precedent — a dated catalyst to diary.
insights.locator: The Wall Street Journal states that the agreement contains a provision

insights.claim: 123 agreement discussions with Riyadh began during the first Trump administration and continued through the Biden administration, making the current deal a case of policy continuity rather than rupture.
insights.speaker: Jennifer T. Gordon
insights.so_what: Bipartisan continuity lowers the odds a future administration unwinds it, extending the planning horizon for participating vendors.
insights.locator: Discussions between Washington and Riyadh over a 123 agreement

insights.claim: Uranium enrichment and plutonium reprocessing are dual-use: the same technology that makes reactor fuel makes weapons fuel, which is why US strategy has been to promote peaceful nuclear use while restricting sensitive fuel-making technology.
insights.speaker: Matthew Kroenig
insights.so_what: The analytical basis for treating enrichment permission, not reactor sales, as the material variable in any nuclear cooperation deal.
insights.locator: Since the dawn of the nuclear age

insights.claim: US nonproliferation policy has been applied to friends and enemies alike: the Pentagon used military force to stop Iran's enrichment program in both 2025 and 2026, while Washington used influence to forestall sensitive fuel-making capability in South Korea, Taiwan and the United Arab Emirates.
insights.speaker: Matthew Kroenig
insights.so_what: Establishes the precedent set that a Saudi carve-out would break, creating a claim other allies could invoke.
insights.locator: Washington’s policy has been successful and imposed on friends and enemies alike

insights.claim: Allowing enrichment in Saudi Arabia would be a mistake, and the two-year study should conclude that Riyadh can rely on imported fuel-cycle services as many other countries with truly peaceful nuclear programs do.
insights.speaker: Matthew Kroenig
insights.so_what: The dissenting position within the US policy establishment — an indicator that the enrichment provision faces real domestic resistance before it can be implemented.
insights.quote: It would be a mistake, therefore, to allow enrichment in Saudi Arabia as part of any deal.
insights.locator: It would be a mistake to allow Saudi Arabia the capability for enrichment

insights.claim: A Saudi enrichment program is not guaranteed because the deal only commits the parties to study whether enriching uranium on Saudi soil would be commercially viable versus relying on imported fuel.
insights.speaker: Matthew Kroenig
insights.so_what: Commercial viability, not just politics, is a gate on Saudi enrichment — enrichment economics at small national scale are unfavorable.
insights.quote: carry out a two-year study to examine the value of enrichment for Saudi Arabia
insights.locator: Fortunately, a Saudi enrichment program is not guaranteed

insights.claim: The Iran war emboldened Tehran and threatened the Gulf, and Saudi Arabia is intent on leveraging the moment to assert regional leadership — with the nuclear deal, renewed Riyadh-Houthi confrontation, and the shifting Saudi-UAE rift all connected to that effort.
insights.speaker: Allison Minor
insights.so_what: Treats three separate Gulf headlines as one strategy — useful for anticipating the next Saudi move rather than reacting to each event in isolation.
insights.locator: The Iran war increased the political urgency for this deal

insights.claim: By keeping the door open for uranium enrichment inside Saudi Arabia, the nuclear deal sends a powerful message to Tehran, and by securing terms apparently more preferable than the UAE and dozens of other US partners accepted, Riyadh signals its status as a major global player.
insights.speaker: Allison Minor
insights.so_what: The deal's value to Riyadh is partly signaling, meaning it may not need to exercise enrichment to extract the benefit.
insights.locator: By keeping the door open for uranium enrichment

insights.claim: The Iran war likely added political urgency to negotiations that had been underway for months as Washington sought to reassure a partner increasingly wary of US security commitments and frustrated by the lack of consultation.
insights.speaker: Allison Minor
insights.so_what: Saudi doubt about US security guarantees is the driver — expect more concessions to Riyadh as long as that doubt persists.
insights.locator: The nuclear deal has been in the works for months

insights.claim: The Biden administration had embedded a Saudi civil nuclear agreement in a larger package including normalization with Israel, a credible pathway to a Palestinian state, and US-Saudi mutual-defense commitments, with a deal nearly finalized in mid-2024 pending an end to the war in Gaza.
insights.speaker: Daniel B. Shapiro
insights.so_what: Establishes the counterfactual price the US could have charged, which is the benchmark for judging what the current deal gave away.
insights.locator: Weighing all these factors, the Biden administration set out

insights.claim: The new agreement has been de-linked from Saudi normalization with Israel, which is not ready to proceed particularly while the current Israeli government is unwilling to engage on a Palestinian state — meaning the US has played a valuable card it could have held back as a normalization incentive.
insights.speaker: Daniel B. Shapiro
insights.so_what: Removes a key catalyst from the Abraham-Accords-expansion thesis; normalization now needs a different and unidentified incentive.
insights.quote: the United States has played a valuable card that could have been held back
insights.locator: The deal has been de-linked from Saudi normalization with Israel

insights.claim: It is not clear whether the Trump administration imposed the same strict safeguards against enrichment that the Biden negotiation had built in, and details have yet to be revealed.
insights.speaker: Daniel B. Shapiro
insights.so_what: The safeguards text is the unknown that determines proliferation impact — the disclosure event to watch.
insights.locator: Now the Trump administration has decided to proceed

insights.claim: A Saudi nuclear capability risks other major Middle East players — Egypt, Turkey and certainly Iran — feeling they must match it, setting off at least a nuclear-technology race and posing potential threats to Israeli security.
insights.speaker: Daniel B. Shapiro
insights.so_what: Names the specific follow-on demand for nuclear technology across the region, and the escalation channel that would raise regional risk premia.
insights.locator: For the United States, it had both pros and cons

insights.claim: If Trump is using the nuclear agreement to smooth over differences with the Saudis over the Iran war or to secure Saudi cooperation in military operations, it would show the US sacrificing one strategic opportunity to plug another strategic hole at a painful opportunity cost.
insights.speaker: Daniel B. Shapiro
insights.so_what: Suggests the deal reflects reduced US leverage rather than strength — a read-through to how much Washington can still extract from Gulf partners.
insights.quote: the United States is prepared to sacrifice one strategic opportunity in order to plug another strategic hole
insights.locator: Perhaps the Trump administration is using this agreement
